column4: This is the section's controlling parallel: rain fills valleys بِقَدَرِهَا, the flood carries زَبَدًا, metalworking raises like foam, and what benefits people يَمْكُثُ while the foam goes away.
The blast makes the destroyed people غُثَاءً; the exact word used for 87:5 here bears its flood-scum sense, turning the disregarded floating refuse into a fate.
Water descends from heaven بِقَدَرٍ, is lodged in the earth, and can be taken away; it joins the section's measure, retained water, and possibility of loss in one scene.
A struck stone releases twelve springs and each people عَلِمَ its drinking place; this meets both the source dictionary's water-holding rock hollow and its ʿ-l-m family image of a water-rich well.
The rock sends out twelve springs and every tribe عَلِمَ its drinking place, again bringing the section's rock cavity, abundant water, and the root of “knows” into one scene.
God sends down water, conducts it as springs within the earth, then the plants yellow and become حُطَامًا; stored water and passing plant refuse form the section's two faces here.
The worldly-life parable begins with rain and mixed vegetation and ends as هَشِيمًا scattered by winds, a direct nonlexical counterpart to useful water outlasting disregarded dry growth.
Earth bursts into springs and the waters meet for an affair already قُدِرَ; gathered floodwater and measure coincide as they do in the section.
Earth is commanded to swallow its water, heaven to cease, and the floodwater subsides; the verse stages where overwhelming water goes and how it is withdrawn.
Paradise contains rivers of مَاءٍ غَيْرِ آسِنٍ, water whose state does not alter; it literalizes the source definition of permanence as remaining in an original condition.
Steadfastness on the way is answered with مَاءً غَدَقًا, abundant water; the moral condition and plentiful provision meet the section's water-rich lexical senses.
The same ayah names ships running بِمَا يَنفَعُ ٱلنَّاسَ and water sent from heaven to revive earth, joining the section's root of benefit to beneficial rain.
All things have divine خزائن and descend only بِقَدَرٍ مَعْلُومٍ; this states the hidden provision and measured release presupposed by the section's retained water.
After 15:21's measured storehouses, this ayah sends fertilizing winds, gives water to drink, and says humans are not its keepers; its own contribution is the water and the limit on human storage.
Water comes from heaven بِقَدَرٍ and revives a dead land, a direct meeting of measured water, useful growth, and return from lifelessness.
The command وَذَكِّرْ is justified because remembrance تَنفَعُ believers, directly completing 87:9's conditional link between reminder and benefit.
The overlooked man may remember فَتَنفَعَهُ ٱلذِّكْرَىٰ; this gives a human scene for the section's image of a reminder becoming retained benefit.
The Prophet is told to remind with the Quran the one who fears the warning, matching 87:9–10's command and its receptive, fearing hearer.
The revelation is specifically تَذْكِرَةً لِّمَن يَخْشَىٰ, the same reminder-and-fear relation that makes the section's offered water useful rather than lost.
A reminder exists for one who has a heart or listens attentively; the receptive hearer supplies the human analogue to a hollow that holds useful water.
Following the overflowing water and rescue of 69:11, the event is made a تَذْكِرَةً retained by an attentive ear; this ayah contributes the explicit meeting of flood and held reminder.
تَجْهَرْ is set against السِّرَّ وَأَخْفَىٰ under God's knowledge, almost reproducing 87:7 while the source section opens j-h-r into the image of clearing mud until water appears.
God يَعْلَمُ both سِرَّكُمْ and جَهْرَكُمْ; the roots of “knows” and “manifest” meet in the same open/hidden relation from which the section derives its well image.
God knows ٱلْجَهْرَ مِنَ ٱلْقَوْلِ and what people conceal, directly pairing the source section's j-h-r root with knowing the hidden.
Whether speech is concealed or made public with ٱجْهَرُوا, God knows what breasts contain; disclosure and hidden knowledge again form the well-clearing analogy's conceptual frame.
مَا عِندَكُمْ يَنفَدُ وَمَا عِندَ ٱللَّهِ بَاقٍ states in bare terms the section's division between what runs out and what remains.
The fading زَهْرَةَ ٱلْحَيَوٰةِ ٱلدُّنْيَا is set against the Lord's provision as خَيْرٌ وَأَبْقَىٰ, joining vegetation, divine provision, goodness, and permanence.
Worldly wealth and children are adornment, while ٱلْبَاقِيَاتُ ٱلصَّالِحَاتُ are better with the Lord; it names the morally valuable remainder behind the water image.
After guidance increases, ٱلْبَاقِيَاتُ ٱلصَّالِحَاتُ are declared better in reward and return, linking reception of guidance to what endures.
Worldly goods are temporary enjoyment and adornment, while what is with God is خَيْرٌ وَأَبْقَىٰ, exactly the section's better-and-lasting axis.
Worldly possessions are merely temporary enjoyment, but what is with God is خَيْرٌ وَأَبْقَىٰ for believers who trust their Lord.
The magicians reject Pharaoh's coercion with وَٱللَّهُ خَيْرٌ وَأَبْقَىٰ, making “better and more lasting” an enacted choice rather than an abstraction.
بَقِيَّتُ ٱللَّهِ خَيْرٌ لَّكُمْ makes a God-given lawful remainder better than gain taken by fraud, a social form of beneficial residue.
كُلُّ مَنْ عَلَيْهَا فَانٍ gives the vanishing side of the section's distinction at the scale of all earthly life.
After 55:26 says all earthly life passes, this ayah contributes the abiding وَجْهُ رَبِّكَ, the enduring side of the pair.
Truth arrives and falsehood is زَهُوقًا, destined to vanish; it states directly what 13:17 makes visible through disappearing foam.
Truth is cast against falsehood until it crushes it and falsehood is زَاهِقٌ, another direct verbal statement of the foam parable's moral action.
A good word is a good tree whose root is ثابت, giving the section's beneficial remainder a stable vegetal counterpart.
The stable tree of 14:24 continually gives fruit by its Lord's permission; this ayah contributes the lasting thing's recurring benefit.
The corrupt word is a bad tree uprooted from the earth with no قرار, the vegetal opposite of both held water and what remains in the ground.
Rain-grown vegetation pleases, then yellows and becomes حُطَامًا while worldly life is deceptive enjoyment; it closely restages growth turning into disregarded debris.
The parable of worldly life begins with heavenly water and luxuriant growth, then leaves the land harvested as though it had not flourished, emphasizing passing appearance.
Iron is sent with great force and مَنَافِعُ لِلنَّاسِ; this joins 13:17's worked metal for useful objects to the section's root of benefit.
Iron is heated until it is firelike and molten copper is poured over it, directly restaging the metal-and-fire half of the foam parable.
David is told to make armor and قَدِّرْ فِى ٱلسَّرْدِ, bringing useful metalwork and exact measure together as 13:17 does.
God sends مَاءً طَهُورًا from heaven; its purity directly answers the source dictionary's well cleared until the water appears and becomes clear.
The pure water of 25:48 revives dead land and gives drink to cattle and people; this ayah contributes the water's concrete benefit.
Earth brings forth مَاءَهَا وَمَرْعَىٰهَا, placing water and pasture side by side as the section's flood, held rain, and dry herbage require.
A well-placed garden gives doubled produce under a downpour and still yields under drizzle, making retained rain an image of expenditure that truly benefits.
Where 13:17's flood carries disregarded foam, overflowing water here carries and preserves the ancestors in the ark; the shared carrying action marks what the water discards versus saves.
A downpour strips soil from a smooth rock and leaves it bare, so ostentatious spending yields nothing; this reverses the source image of a rock hollow retaining beneficial rain.
Rocks here gush rivers or split so water comes out, reversing the dictionary image in which a hollow in rock receives and holds water from heaven.
Garden water may become غَوْرًا, sunk beyond recovery; it supplies the explicit opposite of water lodged accessibly in earth or a rock hollow.
If water sinks away, no one can bring مَاءٍ مَّعِينٍ; accessible flowing water is set against hidden, irretrievable water.
The good land yields plants by its Lord's leave while bad land yields only scantily, showing that the same water does not become retained benefit in every receiver.
A thirsty person takes a mirage for water and finds nothing there, the perceptual opposite of the section's real, useful water that remains.
A بِئْرٍ مُّعَطَّلَةٍ is an abandoned well amid ruined settlements, the direct opposite of the source dictionary's water-rich well.
كُلُّ شَىْءٍ هَالِكٌ إِلَّا وَجْهَهُ draws the ultimate boundary between perishing things and the one abiding reality.
God could make cloud-water أُجَاجًا, bitter; this marks the boundary between mere remaining liquid and the beneficial water the section values.
Wine and gambling contain مَنَافِعُ, yet their sin is greater than their benefit; this qualifies the source definition by showing that an isolated benefit need not lead to good.
The Quran is healing and mercy for believers but increases wrongdoers only in loss, clarifying 87:9's condition that a reminder must actually benefit its receiver.
The revelation is guidance and healing for believers but deafness and blindness for others, another precise boundary between water-like benefit and failed reception.
Immediately before the flood parable, this ayah identifies رَبُّ ٱلسَّمَاوَاتِ وَٱلْأَرْضِ as God; it lets the source's r-b-b family image of gathered abundant water meet 13:17's sender of rain.
Within the approach to 13:17, hidden speech and one who جَهَرَ بِهِ are equally known; the ayah supplies the open/hidden root relation used by the section's well-clearing sense.
Directly after the flood parable, this ayah distinguishes those who answer their Lord from those who do not; it applies the useful-versus-lost distinction to reception.
Following 67:13's concealed and public speech, this ayah asks whether the One who خَلَقَ would not know, joining the section's creation and knowledge roots around hiddenness.
The prayer addresses رَبَّنَا as knowing what people hide and disclose, combining the Lord root with the same concealed/revealed knowledge behind the clear-water image.

The Quranic ٱلْحَوَايَا means entrails in a dietary ruling; the source section explicitly uses the same dictionary form for winding hollows filled by floodwater, so the bodily sense exposes the shared coiled shape.
The brothers propose casting Joseph into غَيَابَتِ ٱلْجُبِّ, the well's hidden depth; this supplies the concealed-well object behind the source's act of clearing until water appears.
With 12:10 identifying the well, this ayah contributes the water-drawer and lowered bucket; what the well reveals is Joseph, an apt reversal of uncovering hidden water.

On the reading reflected by حَمِئَةٍ, the sun is found setting at a muddy spring; that mud-and-water conjunction recalls the source's well whose water is obscured by mud, though the ayah is not about cleaning it.
Heaven's gates open with pouring water, supplying the descending half of the flood scene that 54:12 completes when earth's springs meet it.
إِنَّا كُلَّ شَىْءٍ خَلَقْنَاهُ بِقَدَرٍ joins creation and measure exactly as 87:2–3 do, while nearby 54:11–12 embody that measure in floodwater.
God خَلَقَ everything and فَقَدَّرَهُ تَقْدِيرًا; the same creation-measure sequence underlies the capacities of the section's valleys and hollows.
Provision is sent down بِقَدَرٍ because unrestricted plenty would corrupt, giving the section's measured provision a stated moral reason.
Heavenly water provides both drink and vegetation in which livestock graze, joining useful water to pasture before it can become dry refuse.
Water from heaven brings forth diverse pairs of plants, the growth stage presupposed by the section's dry vegetation and flood-borne debris.
After 20:53's rain-grown plants, people are told to eat and pasture their cattle; this ayah contributes the vegetation's human and animal benefit.
After 79:31 names earth's water and pasture, this ayah identifies them as provision for people and livestock, stating why the retained water matters.
أَنَّا صَبَبْنَا ٱلْمَاءَ صَبًّا presents the forceful pouring of water that begins the section's movement from rain to channels and growth.
Earth is split open after the poured water of 80:25, showing the receiving ground through which useful growth emerges.
Fruit and أَبًّا, herbage or pasture, are among the products of the poured water, linking rain directly to the plant matter later left dry.
The rain-grown foods of 80:27–31 are called provision for people and livestock, making explicit the benefit side of the image.
Blessed water descends from heaven and grows gardens and harvested grain, a compact instance of water becoming lasting provision.
The growth from 50:9 is provision for servants and revives a dead land, stating both benefit and life-giving persistence.
Gardens are given springs flowing through them, a cultivated counterpart to water gathering and remaining in the earth.
The springs and gardens of 36:34 yield fruit for people to eat and invite gratitude; this ayah contributes the retained water's benefit.
The question أَفَرَءَيْتُمُ ٱلْمَاءَ ٱلَّذِى تَشْرَبُونَ directs attention to water precisely as a received benefit.
Humans do not send the water down from ٱلْمُزْنِ, the rain clouds; this supplies the cloud source of the water held in the section's rock hollows.
Water is driven to barren land and brings crops eaten by livestock and people, linking conveyed water, pasture, and concrete benefit.
Clouds are driven, joined, and heaped before rain emerges from them, detailing how the cloud water named by the source dictionary gathers and is released.
Winds carry heavy clouds to dead land, where rain produces every fruit; the scene links gathered cloud water to useful revival.
Iron is made pliable for David, supplying the worked-metal action that stands beside floodwater in 13:17's paired foam image.
A spring of molten copper is made to flow for Solomon, combining liquid movement with the melted metal of 13:17's second comparison.
قُدُورٍ رَّاسِيَاتٍ names fixed cauldrons, the exact vessel behind the source dictionary's secondary phrase “foam of the flood and of the cooking pot,” though this ayah mentions no foam.
Even a mustard-seed hidden inside a صَخْرَةٍ is known and brought forth by God, joining the section's rock cavity to its theme of what is hidden yet known.
Livestock provide مَنَافِعُ وَمَشَارِبُ, putting the benefit root beside things drunk and thereby echoing useful water as provision.
God erases falsehood and confirms truth by His words, a conceptual rendering of the foam being removed while what has value remains.
God establishes truth and nullifies falsehood, expressing the same separation that 13:17 depicts as water or useful metal beneath passing foam.
The deeds of disbelievers are ashes violently scattered by wind and cannot be retained, paralleling the section's disregarded plant refuse that goes away.
Rejected deeds become هَبَاءً مَّنثُورًا, scattered dust; this is another concrete Quranic image for what is dispersed and not counted as benefit.
فَذَكِّرْ إِنَّمَا أَنتَ مُذَكِّرٌ repeats the prophetic stance of offering reminder whose reception determines whether it benefits.
An admonition from the Lord is called healing, guidance, and mercy, specifying the kinds of good that a beneficial reminder helps its hearer reach.
Worldly enjoyment is called little and the hereafter خَيْرٌ for the God-fearing, a concise parallel to the section's better-and-lasting judgment.
Worldly life is temporary enjoyment while the hereafter is دَارُ ٱلْقَرَارِ, the abode of settled permanence rather than passing surface matter.

Immediately after the flood parable and its application in 13:18, this ayah contrasts one who يَعْلَمُ that the revelation is truth with the blind and says only people of understanding remember; it joins knowledge, truth, and receptive remembrance.
Noah says he called his people جِهَارًا, bringing the section's j-h-r root into a prophetic reminder whose failed reception eventually turns rainwater into a destroying flood.
After Noah's open call in 71:8, this ayah contributes his combined public proclamation and secret appeal, a sustained open/hidden preaching stance close to 87:7–10.
As the promised response to accepting Noah's reminder, heaven would send abundant rain; useful descending water is thus set inside the same surah as the later flood of rejection.
Following 71:11's abundant rain, this ayah contributes gardens and rivers among the resulting provisions, making the water's retained benefit explicit.
Even a sea used as ink would run out before the words of رَبِّى run out; finite water is reversed into a measure of the inexhaustible divine word.
A sea replenished by seven more seas still cannot exhaust God's words, giving the passing-water/enduring-word relation an even larger formulation.
The destroyed people become كَهَشِيمِ ٱلْمُحْتَظِرِ, dry broken plant matter, a close nonlexical counterpart to غُثَاء as the disregarded remainder of destruction.
The army is made like عَصْفٍ مَّأْكُولٍ, consumed straw, another Quranic transformation of the rejected into worthless plant debris.
Warning benefits the one who follows the reminder and fears the Merciful unseen, closely repeating 87:9–10's reminder-and-fear condition.
Pouring water descends from the rain clouds, a direct formulation of the cloud-water that the source's rock hollows receive.
After 78:14's pouring rain, this ayah contributes grain and vegetation brought out by it, showing the water becoming useful growth.
This completes 78:14–15 with dense gardens, the lasting cultivated result of descending water.
Paradisal provision is described as having no depletion, a direct formulation of beneficial provision that remains instead of running out.
In the approach to 13:17, one who calls false gods is like a person stretching hands toward water that never reaches the mouth; it is the section's beneficial water rendered present yet unreceived.
After Noah's public and secret calls and the offered rain of 71:8–12, the rejecters are drowned for their sins; water changes from promised provision to judgment when reminder is refused.
The flood saves Noah and those with him in the ark while drowning the deniers, distinguishing what overwhelming water preserves from what it removes.
Noah and his companions are saved in the ark and made successors while the rejecters are drowned, another explicit preservation/removal boundary within one flood.
The condemned are told إِنَّكُم مَّاكِثُونَ, using the same staying root as 13:17 to show that permanence itself is not identical with benefit.

One body of water is fresh and pleasant to drink while another is salty and bitter, yet both yield food and adornment; the verse distinguishes kinds of water and kinds of benefit rather than treating all water alike.

The gold and silver named in 9:34 are heated in hellfire and used to brand their hoarders; this reverses 13:17's fire-worked metal for ornament or useful goods into hoarded metal that becomes punishment.
A freezing wind destroys the crop of people who wrong themselves, reversing the beneficial rain-and-growth sequence and leaving effort without useful yield.
A destroyed people persist in their cry until they are made حَصِيدًا خَامِدِينَ, harvested and extinguished; it parallels people reduced to the dry refuse represented by غُثَاء.
The Prophet is only a warner to the one who fears the Hour, repeating the section's stance that admonition reaches its intended effect in a fearing hearer.
Immediately before 80:4 says reminder may benefit him, this ayah contributes the possibility that the neglected hearer may purify himself.
Dead earth is revived and yields grain for eating; it supplies the revival stage immediately before the gardens and springs of 36:34–35.
Winds raise clouds, God spreads and fragments them, and rain emerges from within; this repeats in detail the collection and release of the cloud-water named by the source.
Winds raise clouds that are driven to dead land and revive it, a repeated formulation of gathered cloud-water becoming useful life.
Water sent from heaven revives dead earth and is called a sign for people who listen, linking water's benefit to receptive hearing.
Heavenly water brings forth green growth, grain, gardens, and fruits; it develops the productive plant side from which dry flood debris later comes.
Rain makes the earth become green, a concise instance of water producing the living surface later contrasted with dried refuse.
A lifeless, humbled earth stirs and swells when water descends, making the water's life-giving benefit visible.
Every living thing is made from water, stating the most basic reason water is the beneficial element beneath the passing surface debris.
Lofty mountains are placed on earth and people are given sweet water to drink, bringing rock, gathered fresh water, and provision into one ayah.
Where 12:10 proposes the hidden depth of the well and 12:19 later lowers the bucket, this ayah contributes the actual placing of Joseph in that concealed hollow.
Moses reaches Midian's watering place and finds a crowd watering livestock while two women hold back, a concrete scene around an abundant shared water source.
After 28:23 identifies the watering place and need, Moses waters the women's flock; this ayah contributes water becoming an immediate act of benefit.
Truth comes and falsehood can neither originate nor restore anything, a further verbal counterpart to the foam parable's vanishing falsehood.
God establishes truth by His words despite the criminals' dislike, corresponding to the enduring truth beneath 13:17's passing foam.
Earth's adornment is destined to become barren ground, a non-water version of luxuriant surface growth ending as lifeless residue.
The later state is declared better than the former, echoing both the section's خَيْرٌ judgment and the “first” language embedded in its definition of permanence.
Worldly life is play and diversion while the hereafter's abode is better for the God-fearing, a repeated formulation of 87:16–17's choice.
Worldly life is play and diversion while the hereafter is the true life, sharpening the section's distinction between passing appearance and enduring reality.
Gold, silver, and other desired goods are named as worldly adornment and temporary enjoyment; these are the ornaments for which 13:17's metals are worked, now placed on the passing side.
This ayah names gold and silver hoarded instead of spent for good, identifying the metal whose heating in 9:35 turns the useful-or-ornamental metal scene into a judgment on withheld benefit.
Water sent from heaven brings fruits as provision and stands beside subjected rivers, another compact sequence from rain to enduring human benefit.
